 Omar Abdullah's Marriage: Time to Celebrate When the Political House is Burning?
 Omar Abdullah has begun a new chapter in his personal life. Jammu and Kashmir is still waiting for a convincing new chapter in governance
 ADV SUNIL SETHI & ALTAF THAKUR 
 03 Nov 2026 02:05 IST
 Follow Us
 Politics has its own sense of timing, and sometimes events unfolding simultaneously reveal more than lengthy political speeches. Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah has begun a new chapter in his personal life with his marriage to journalist Nidhi Razdan on October 30. The occasion deserves congratulations, and nobody has any business questioning his personal choices. But the political circumstances in which this new beginning has taken place raise an uncomfortable question: when the political house is burning, can its captain afford to remain detached from the fire? 
 The National Conference is passing through a particularly turbulent phase. Its recent Cabinet reshuffle, instead of bringing stability, has exposed serious internal differences. Legislators are openly expressing resentment, senior leaders feel marginalised, regional representation has become controversial, and Srinagar MP Aga Ruhullah Mehdi has announced his decision to leave the party and resign from Parliament. 
 Omar Abdullah may have every reason to celebrate his personal happiness, but the people of Jammu and Kashmir have equally compelling reasons to demand answers about the government they elected. 
 The issue is not his marriage. The issue is the political leadership and its priorities. 
 A Cabinet reshuffle that has opened a Pandora's box 
 The Cabinet expansion on October 27 was expected to strengthen the government after nearly two years of functioning with vacancies. Instead, it has generated a wave of dissatisfaction within the ruling party. 
 At least 18 National Conference legislators reportedly assembled in Srinagar to discuss their grievances. Their concerns reportedly extend beyond ministerial accommodation to the functioning of the government, the influence of political advisers, the exclusion of senior leaders and the failure to fulfil electoral commitments. 
 Some legislators have questioned why people without an electoral mandate enjoy significant access to the Chief Minister while elected representatives struggle to secure an effective voice in decision-making. 
 The public dissatisfaction expressed by senior leaders such as Mubarak Gul and Abdul Majid Larmi has further exposed the depth of the problem. 
 This is no longer simply a question of who became a minister and who did not. It is a question of whether the elected representatives of the National Conference have confidence in the political management of their own government. 
 A Chief Minister who cannot adequately address the grievances of his own legislators will inevitably face questions about his ability to maintain political cohesion. 
 The Abdullah family's political inheritance under scrutiny 
 The National Conference has a long history and a political legacy associated with Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah and subsequently Farooq Abdullah. But political inheritance cannot become a permanent substitute for organisational democracy. 
 The party's present predicament raises questions about the concentration of political authority around the Abdullah family and the limited space available to independent voices. 
 Aga Ruhullah Mehdi's announced departure has added another dimension to this debate. His public criticism, including his allegation that the party treats Jammu and Kashmir like a family estate, is particularly damaging because it comes from within the National Conference's own political ranks. 
 His objections concern unfulfilled electoral commitments and the leadership's approach to political accountability. 
 The National Conference may disagree with his assessment, but it cannot ignore the political significance of a sitting MP publicly distancing himself from the party leadership. 
 When legislators and elected representatives begin questioning the political culture of their own organisation, the leadership must recognise that the problem extends beyond individual ambitions. 
 Jammu's political exclusion 
 The Cabinet reshuffle has also revived an old and sensitive question: does Jammu receive adequate political representation in a government elected to administer the entire Union Territory? 
 The dropping of Satish Sharma has left the Jammu plains without representation in the Council of Ministers. The erstwhile Doda District also continues to remain unrepresented. 
 For a region that has repeatedly complained about political neglect, this development has naturally generated resentment. 
 The National Conference cannot seek votes across Jammu and Kashmir and then treat regional representation as a secondary consideration while distributing political power. 
 Jammu's concerns are not about demanding special privileges. They are about democratic representation, dignity and equal participation in governance. 
 Omar Abdullah must explain why the Cabinet's composition has generated such widespread regional dissatisfaction. The government cannot expect people to accept political imbalance merely because the Chief Minister considers the reshuffle an internal administrative decision. 
 Election promises: Where is the accountability? 
 The National Conference secured its mandate in 2024 on a series of significant political and economic commitments. Restoration of statehood, protection of rights, employment opportunities and relief on economic concerns were central to the party's campaign. 
 Two years later, people are entitled to ask what has actually been delivered. 
 The most uncomfortable aspect for Omar Abdullah is that questions about these promises are now emerging from within his own party. Aga Ruhullah's criticism has brought the issue of political credibility into sharp focus. 
 An election manifesto is not a document to be remembered only during campaigning. It represents a commitment to the electorate. 
 The Chief Minister must provide a transparent account of the commitments fulfilled, those still pending and the reasons for delays. 
 The people of Jammu and Kashmir did not elect a government merely to witness a change in political personalities. They expected meaningful governance and measurable results. 
 Celebrations cannot replace political responsibility 
 Omar Abdullah's marriage is a private milestone. But his public office carries responsibilities that cannot be put on hold. 
 The Chief Minister must address the growing dissatisfaction among legislators, explain the rationale behind the Cabinet reshuffle, respond to regional concerns and restore confidence among people who supported his party. 
 The National Conference cannot afford to treat every disagreement as a conspiracy or every dissatisfied legislator as an opponent of the leadership. 
 Democratic organisations survive through consultation, accommodation and accountability, not through unquestioning loyalty to individuals. 
 There is also a larger political irony. The party that frequently invokes its historical legacy and claims to represent the aspirations of Jammu and Kashmir must now answer questions about its own internal democratic functioning. 
 The BJP, as the principal opposition, will naturally examine these developments and question the government's performance. But the ultimate accountability is not to the opposition; it is to the electorate. 
 The morning after the celebrations 
 The wedding celebrations will eventually end. The guests will return, the photographs will become memories and the couple will embark on their new journey. 
 But the political crisis will not disappear with the celebrations. 
 The disgruntled legislators will still expect answers. Jammu will continue to demand adequate representation. The announced departure of Aga Ruhullah will remain a serious political development. The electorate will continue asking about promises that have yet to translate into results. 
 Omar Abdullah must now demonstrate that he can manage the responsibilities of the government through consultation and political accountability rather than relying exclusively on the authority of his office and his family's legacy. 
 A Chief Minister's greatest political achievement is not the management of party positions or the preservation of family influence. It is the confidence he commands among the people he governs. 
 There is nothing wrong with celebrating a new beginning in personal life. But when the political house is burning, the responsibility of its captain is to extinguish the fire before it consumes the entire establishment. 
 Omar Abdullah has begun a new chapter in his personal life. Jammu and Kashmir is still waiting for a convincing new chapter in governance. 
 (Sunil Sethi is Chief Spokesperson, JK BJP and   Altaf Thakur is Spokesperson, JK BJP)
